Proposition 3.1 (Well-posedness and stationarity of the conditional phase space process) . For every fixed y,\widetilde{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and initial phase space point (x_{0},p_{0}) , the event-driven dynamics in Algorithm 1 , with the reference point fixed at \widetilde{x} , defines a unique non-explosive, time-homogeneous Markov process. The phase space measure \nu_{\eta,y} is stationary for this process. In particular, the returned position x_{\pi} is well-defined almost surely.
Fix y,\widetilde{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} . In the notation of ( 3.4 ), the bounce rate ( 3.9 ) reads

The bounce map is an involution. Although there is a possible discontinuity at h_{\widetilde{x}}(x)=0 , this creates no ambiguity because the event rate vanishes there.

Finally, the memoryless property of the exponential clocks gives the time-homogeneous Markov property. This is precisely the integrated hazard construction of Davis [ 12 , Section 2] . ∎

With the process now constructed, we prove the stationarity assertion in Proposition 3.1 and record the stronger operator facts used to analyze the averaged kernel. Recall \nu_{\eta,y} from ( 3.1 ), and define momentum reversal by
\mathsf{R}(x,p)\coloneqq(x,-p)\,,\hskip 20.00003pt(\mathsf{R}F)(x,p)\coloneqq F(\mathsf{R}(x,p))\,.
As usual, we use the same symbol for \nu_{\eta,y} and its Lebesgue density:
\nu_{\eta,y}(x,p)\propto\exp\Bigl\{-V_{y}(x)-\frac{\|p\|^{2}}{2}\Bigr\}\,.
The identity ( A.3 ) is a momentum-reversed form of detailed balance. To see the mechanism formally, write \mathsf{L}_{y,\widetilde{x}}=\mathcal{A}+\mathcal{J} , where
Momentum reversal reverses the harmonic flow, so \mathsf{R}\mathcal{A}\mathsf{R}=-\mathcal{A} . Moreover,
\mathcal{A}\log\nu_{\eta,y}(x,p)=-\sqrt{\eta}\,p^{\top}h_{\widetilde{x}}(x)=-\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}(x,p)+\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}(x,-p).
Formal integration by parts gives
\mathcal{A}^{*}=-\mathcal{A}+\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}-\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}\circ\mathsf{R}.

The bounce map \mathsf{S}_{\widetilde{x}} is a \nu_{\eta,y} -preserving involution, commutes with \mathsf{R} , and satisfies \lambda_{\widetilde{x}}\circ\mathsf{S}_{\widetilde{x}}=\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}\circ\mathsf{R} . A formal change of variables therefore gives
\mathcal{J}^{*}G=(\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}\circ\mathsf{R})(G\circ\mathsf{S}_{\widetilde{x}})-\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}G.
Combining the two identities yields
\mathsf{L}_{y,\widetilde{x}}^{*}G=-\mathcal{A}G+(\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}\circ\mathsf{R})(G\circ\mathsf{S}_{\widetilde{x}}-G)=(\mathsf{R}\mathsf{L}_{y,\widetilde{x}}\mathsf{R})G.

Formally exponentiating this identity gives (\mathsf{T}_{t}^{y,\widetilde{x}})^{*}=\mathsf{R}\mathsf{T}_{t}^{y,\widetilde{x}}\mathsf{R} ; Gaussian momentum averaging then removes \mathsf{R} and produces an ordinary self-adjoint position kernel.

This generator calculation is only heuristic as stated, as the standard arguments are not immediately applicable because \mathsf{S}_{\widetilde{x}} may be discontinuous where h_{\widetilde{x}}(x)=0 . The pathwise argument below proves the same identity without requiring differentiability or continuity of the bounce map.
Along \zeta_{s}=(x_{s},p_{s})=\Phi_{s}^{y,\widetilde{x}}(\zeta_{0}) ,

\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}s}\log\nu_{\eta,y}(\zeta_{s})=-\sqrt{\eta}\,p_{s}^{\top}h_{\widetilde{x}}(x_{s})=-\bigl\{\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}(\zeta_{s})-\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}(\mathsf{R}\zeta_{s})\bigr\}\,. (A.4)
Moreover, by definition of \mathsf{R} and \Phi_{t} ,
\mathsf{R}\Phi_{t}^{y,\widetilde{x}}\mathsf{R}=\Phi_{-t}^{y,\widetilde{x}}\,,\hskip 20.00003pt\mathsf{R}\mathsf{S}_{\widetilde{x}}=\mathsf{S}_{\widetilde{x}}\mathsf{R}\,.
If \zeta^{+}=\mathsf{S}_{\widetilde{x}}\zeta^{-} is a non-trivial jump, then h_{\widetilde{x}}(x)\neq 0 , (p^{-})^{\top}h_{\widetilde{x}}(x)>0 , and
\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}(\zeta^{-})=\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}(\mathsf{R}\zeta^{+})\,. (A.5)
The flow and \mathsf{R} preserve Lebesgue measure, as does the possibly discontinuous bounce map: by Fubini’s theorem and orthogonality, for every integrable F ,
\int F(\mathsf{S}_{\widetilde{x}}(x,p))\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}p=\int F(x,p)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}p\,. (A.6)
To pass from these identities to complete trajectories, let
\Delta_{n}(t)\coloneqq\{(t_{1},\ldots,t_{n}):0<t_{1}<\cdots<t_{n}<t\}\,.

Given \zeta_{0} and \mathbf{t}\in\Delta_{n}(t) , let \zeta_{s}^{\zeta_{0},\mathbf{t}} be the path obtained by following \Phi^{y,\widetilde{x}} and applying \mathsf{S}_{\widetilde{x}} at the prescribed times. Iterating the exponential clock construction gives, for every bounded measurable functional \Psi of the path up to time t ,

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\zeta_{0}}\Psi(\zeta_{[0,t]}) \displaystyle=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\int_{\Delta_{n}(t)}\Psi(\zeta_{[0,t]}^{\zeta_{0},\mathbf{t}})\exp\Bigl\{-\!\int_{0}^{t}\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}(\zeta_{s}^{\zeta_{0},\mathbf{t}})\,\mathrm{d}s\Bigr\}\prod_{j=1}^{n}\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}(\zeta_{t_{j}-}^{\zeta_{0},\mathbf{t}})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{t}\,. (A.7)

The series is absolutely convergent because \lvert\Delta_{n}(t)\rvert=t^{n}/n! and the rate is bounded by \bar{\lambda}_{\mathcal{E}}(y,\widetilde{x}) . Integrate ( A.7 ) against \nu_{\eta,y}(\mathrm{d}\zeta_{0}) and apply
(\zeta_{s})_{0\leq s\leq t}\longmapsto(\mathsf{R}\zeta_{t-s})_{0\leq s\leq t}\,,\hskip 20.00003pt(t_{1},\ldots,t_{n})\longmapsto(t-t_{n},\ldots,t-t_{1})\,. (A.8)

For completeness, we justify this change of variables despite the possible discontinuity of the bounce map. For fixed \mathbf{t}\in\Delta_{n}(t) , the endpoint map \zeta_{0}\mapsto\zeta_{t}^{\zeta_{0},\mathbf{t}} is a finite composition of the Borel involution \mathsf{S}_{\widetilde{x}} and the affine harmonic flows \Phi_{u}^{y,\widetilde{x}} . By ( A.6 ) and the explicit flow formula, each factor is a measure-preserving Borel bijection. Hence the endpoint map, and therefore \zeta_{0}\mapsto\mathsf{R}\zeta_{t}^{\zeta_{0},\mathbf{t}} , is a Borel measure-preserving bijection. The identities preceding ( A.7 ) show that its inverse is obtained by using the reversed ordered times in ( A.8 ). The map on \Delta_{n}(t) is linear with absolute determinant one. Thus the full change of variables is measure preserving; no Jacobian is needed.
Integrating ( A.4 ) over the deterministic arcs and using that a reflection preserves \nu_{\eta,y} gives
\nu_{\eta,y}(\zeta_{0})\,e^{-\int_{0}^{t}\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}(\zeta_{s})\,\mathrm{d}s}=\nu_{\eta,y}(\zeta_{t})\,e^{-\int_{0}^{t}\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}(\mathsf{R}\zeta_{s})\,\mathrm{d}s}\,.

This identity matches the initial density and survival factor of a forward path with those of its reversal, while ( A.5 ) matches every jump-rate factor. Hence, each n -jump term in ( A.7 ) is unchanged by ( A.8 ). Tonelli’s theorem justifies the termwise change of variables for non-negative bounded functions; decomposing signed functions into positive and negative parts then gives, for bounded measurable F,G ,
\int F\,\mathsf{T}_{t}^{y,\widetilde{x}}G\,\mathrm{d}\nu_{\eta,y}=\int(\mathsf{R}G)\,\mathsf{T}_{t}^{y,\widetilde{x}}(\mathsf{R}F)\,\mathrm{d}\nu_{\eta,y}\,.
Taking F=1 proves invariance, and the identity extends by density to ( A.3 ) on L^{2}(\nu_{\eta,y}) .

Invariance and Jensen’s inequality give \|\mathsf{T}_{t}^{y,\widetilde{x}}F\|_{2}\leq\|F\|_{2} . It remains to prove strong continuity. For F\in C_{\rm c}(\mathbb{R}^{2d}) , the deterministic flow converges to the identity as t\searrow 0 , and the probability of a jump before time t is
1-\exp\Bigl\{-\int_{0}^{t}\lambda_{\widetilde{x}}(\Phi_{s}^{y,\widetilde{x}}\zeta)\,\mathrm{d}s\Bigr\}\longrightarrow 0\,.
Dominated convergence therefore gives \mathsf{T}_{t}^{y,\widetilde{x}}F\to F in L^{2} . Density of C_{\rm c}(\mathbb{R}^{2d}) and contractivity extend this to all F\in L^{2} .
Finally, Gaussian momentum averaging satisfies \mathsf{R}\mathsf{\Pi}_{p}^{*}=\mathsf{\Pi}_{p}^{*} and \mathsf{\Pi}_{p}\mathsf{R}=\mathsf{\Pi}_{p} . Combining these identities with ( A.3 ) gives

(\mathsf{\Pi}_{p}\mathsf{T}_{t}^{y,\widetilde{x}}\mathsf{\Pi}_{p}^{*})^{*}=\mathsf{\Pi}_{p}(\mathsf{T}_{t}^{y,\widetilde{x}})^{*}\mathsf{\Pi}_{p}^{*}=\mathsf{\Pi}_{p}\mathsf{R}\mathsf{T}_{t}^{y,\widetilde{x}}\mathsf{R}\mathsf{\Pi}_{p}^{*}=\mathsf{\Pi}_{p}\mathsf{T}_{t}^{y,\widetilde{x}}\mathsf{\Pi}_{p}^{*}\,.
This proves self-adjointness; the Markov and contraction properties are inherited from \mathsf{T}_{t}^{y,\widetilde{x}} . ∎

Since \nabla V is continuous, the harmonic flow, event rate, and reflection map are jointly Borel; the convention R_{0}=I ensures this even where the reflection normal vanishes. The integrated hazard is jointly Borel, with continuous, nondecreasing dependence on time, so its threshold-crossing times are Borel, as can be checked using rational times. Thus the recursion ( A.1 )–( A.2 ) makes each jump time and post-jump state Borel in (y,x_{0},p_{0},\widetilde{x},(E_{j})_{j\geq 1}) . By non-explosion, the terminal state at time \pi is the almost-sure limit of the Borel terminal states obtained by allowing at most n jumps. Setting the limit to zero wherever it does not exist gives a Borel version.

The conditional density in ( 2.8 ) is jointly Borel in (y,\widetilde{x}) . Integrating \mathbf{1}_{\{x_{\pi}\in A\}} against this reference law and the laws of the Gaussian momentum and exponential clocks therefore makes (y,x)\mapsto\mathcal{H}_{y}(x,A) Borel for every Borel set A .
